## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#the-same-t-within-an-analyst}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Everyone who chose the same analyst got **the same *t***, to the third decimal, on different machines. That is reproducibility, and once the data and the code are in hand it is the cheap R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The analysts did not get the same *t*: −3.804, −7.169 and −1.206, on one claim, under one set of instructions.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None was careless. The numbers differ because they made different choices about the **data** (which unemployment series, which respondents), the **model** (which fixed effects) and the **code** (one wave appended twice).
:::
::::

::: notes
Look at what just happened. Everyone who chose the same analyst landed on the same number, to the third decimal, on different machines. [advance] Now look across the groups. Minus three point eight, minus seven point two and minus one point two, for one claim, from analysts who were given the same four instructions. [advance] None was careless. The numbers differ because of choices. About the data: KQXUE measured unemployment as a share of the whole population aged twenty to sixty-four, not of the labour force, and left out the respondents who mentioned nothing, where I scored them zero. About the model: a fixed effect for each country but none for the year, where mine has both. About the code: the Stata script appended one wave twice, and my own first build read one wave twice too, corrected before Multi100 recorded the value. Such choices are what robustness, the second R, is about.
:::

## Three models side by side {#three-models-side-by-side .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Analyst | Model | What it compares | Conventional *t* |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | fixed effects for country and year | each country with itself, after the change common to all countries in a year | −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | a fixed effect for each country | each country with itself, the common change included | −7.169 on 242 df |
| 018OL | random intercepts for country, year and wave | change within countries and differences between them at once | −1.206 on 396.9 df |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Between the 27 country means the slope is +`r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_between, 4)`, within countries `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_within, 4)`: a model that blends the two comparisons, as random intercepts do, assumes them equal, and the within–between model rejects that (p = `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$p_difference)`).
:::

::: {.src}
Table and fragment as on the one-day deck (`_segments/eu-frames/_p3-three-models.qmd`); `cases/eu-frames/data/display_between_within.csv`.
:::

::: notes
The two models that you reproduced are two of the three estimators that the menu is built around, beside the third, which the lab offers and we skipped. My model has fixed effects for country and for year, so each country is compared with itself net of whatever all of Europe went through in a year. KQXUE has a fixed effect for each country only, so the common change stays in the comparison. 018OL has random intercepts for country, year and wave, which use the change within countries and the differences between them. [advance] On this panel those two comparisons point in opposite directions: across the country means the slope is slightly positive, within countries it is negative, and the within–between model rejects the equality that random intercepts assume. That is one reason why the three t-values are so far apart, the decision that the second half calls the Estimator.
:::

## Twenty-seven clusters {#twenty-seven-clusters .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Test | Two-way fixed effects (C6HJR) | Country fixed effects, on the course panel |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Conventional | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("conventional", "t"), 2)` on `r inference_of("conventional", "df")` df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("conventional", "p"), 4)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "conventional"], 2)` on `r disp_inference$df[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "conventional"]` df |
| Clustered by country, CR1 | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr1_g1", "t"), 2)` on 26 df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr1_g1", "p"), 3)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr1_g1"], 2)` on 26 df |
| Clustered, CR2, Satterthwaite df | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "t"), 2)` on `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 1)` df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 2)` on `r fmt_num(disp_inference$df[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 1)` df, p = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$p[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 4)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The estimate is the same in every row; only the test changes. The years of one country are not independent, 27 countries are few clusters of unequal weight, and the CR2 test with Satterthwaite df, which classes every point of the curve, counts the countries that effectively carry the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
@BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard; @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust; `cases/eu-frames/data/display_inference.csv`, as on the one-day deck.
:::

::: notes
Now the question that conventional errors avoid. Both reproduced t-values treat each row as independent evidence, but the years of one country resemble each other. Clustering by country allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and the evidence then rests on twenty-seven countries rather than two hundred and seventy rows. With so few clusters, of very unequal weight, the usual clustered test is still too generous, so the course uses the CR2 correction, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom that count how many countries effectively carry the information, fewer than ten here. Read my row: the same estimate goes from a p of two in ten thousand to just above point zero five. Read the row of the design of KQXUE on the course panel: it stays significant under every test. [advance] The estimate never moves, only the test does, and the CR2 test classes every point of the curve.
:::
